claim: Chlamydomonas reinhardtii is a single-celled green algae with two flagella.
source: The single-celled green algae Chlamydomonas reinhardtii with its two flagella—microtubule-based structures of equal and constant lengths—is the canonical model organism for studying size control of organelles.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract as a description of the organism.

claim: The two flagella of Chlamydomonas reinhardtii are microtubule-based structures of equal and constant lengths.
source: The single-celled green algae Chlamydomonas reinhardtii with its two flagella—microtubule-based structures of equal and constant lengths—is the canonical model organism for studying size control of organelles.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract describing the flagellar properties.

claim: Chlamydomonas reinhardtii is the canonical model organism for studying size control of organelles.
source: The single-celled green algae Chlamydomonas reinhardtii with its two flagella—microtubule-based structures of equal and constant lengths—is the canonical model organism for studying size control of organelles.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about the organism's use in research.

claim: Experiments have identified motor-driven transport of tubulin to the flagella tips as a key component of flagellar length control.
source: Experiments have identified motor-driven transport of tubulin to the flagella tips as a key component of their length control.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a summary of experimental findings.

claim: Proteins responsible for intraflagellar transport (IFT) of tubulin are present in limiting amounts.
source: Here we consider a class of models whose key assumption is that proteins responsible for the intraflagellar transport (IFT) of tubulin are present in limiting amounts.
evidence: Stated as a key assumption of the models considered in this work.

claim: The limiting-pool assumption is insufficient to describe the results of severing experiments.
source: We show that the limiting-pool assumption is insufficient to describe the results of severing experiments, in which a flagellum is regenerated after it has been severed.
evidence: Stated as a main finding of the theoretical analysis in the abstract.

claim: The active disassembly model of flagellar length control explains in quantitative detail the results of severing experiments.
source: We show that this 'active disassembly' model of flagellar length control explains in quantitative detail the results of severing experiments and use it to make predictions that can be tested in experiments.
evidence: Stated as a main finding in the abstract, supported by model fitting to experimental data.

claim: Nuclear size is tightly coupled with cell size across a wide range of species.
source: For example, nuclear size is tightly coupled with cell size across a wide range of species (Hara and Merten, 2015) and the loss of this coupling mechanism is implicated in various types of cancer (Zink et al., 2004).
evidence: Stated with citation to support the claim.

claim: Loss of nuclear size-cell size coupling is implicated in various types of cancer.
source: For example, nuclear size is tightly coupled with cell size across a wide range of species (Hara and Merten, 2015) and the loss of this coupling mechanism is implicated in various types of cancer (Zink et al., 2004).
evidence: Stated with citation to support the claim.

claim: Chlamydomonas reinhardtii uses two flagella to move through its aqueous environment.
source: A striking example of organelle size control in eukaryotes is the single-celled algae Chlamydomonas reinhardtii (Figure 1), which uses two flagella to move through its aqueous environment.
evidence: Stated directly in the introduction describing the organism's locomotion.

claim: The backbone of each flagellum is an assembly known as the axoneme that consists of nine microtubule doublets arranged in a ring around a central pair of microtubules.
source: The backbone of each flagellum is an assembly known as the axoneme that consists of nine microtubule doublets arranged in a ring around a central pair of microtubules (Fawcett and Porter, 1954; Witman et al., 1972).
evidence: Stated with citations to support the structural description.

claim: Microtubules in the axoneme exist in a highly stable state, unlike the dynamic instability of cytoplasmic microtubules.
source: Unlike the dynamic instability of cytoplasmic microtubules, which can alternate between rapidly shortening 'catastrophe' and stable 'rescue' states depending on whether or not the tip is bound to GTP, microtubules in the axoneme exist in a highly stable state (Behnke and Forer, 1967; Orbach and Howard, 2019).
evidence: Stated with citations comparing axonemal and cytoplasmic microtubules.

claim: Mutants with longer flagella have decreased swimming velocities and beat frequencies compared to wild type cells.
source: This stability reflects a tight control over flagellar lengths, the loss of which has dramatic physiological consequences; mutants with longer flagella have decreased swimming velocities and beat frequencies (Khona et al., 2013) compared to wild type cells and mutants with unequal flagellar lengths are observed to spin around in circles (Tam et al., 2003).
evidence: Stated with citation to experimental observations.

claim: Mutants with unequal flagellar lengths are observed to spin around in circles.
source: This stability reflects a tight control over flagellar lengths, the loss of which has dramatic physiological consequences; mutants with longer flagella have decreased swimming velocities and beat frequencies (Khona et al., 2013) compared to wild type cells and mutants with unequal flagellar lengths are observed to spin around in circles (Tam et al., 2003).
evidence: Stated with citation to experimental observations.

claim: After one flagellum is severed, the two flagella equalize at a shorter length and then grow together to the original steady-state length.
source: Severing experiments: after one flagellum is severed, the two flagella equalize at a shorter length and then grow together to the original steady-state length. This is demonstrated in experimental data of 20 severing experiments from Ludington et al. (2012) provided by the authors.
evidence: Stated in figure caption and shown in Figure 1b with experimental data.

claim: Intraflagellar transport (IFT) involves continual transport of proteins from the flagellar base to tip and back.
source: A key process contributing to the assembly of flagella is the continual transport of proteins from the flagellar base to tip and back.
evidence: Stated as a description of the IFT process.

claim: Evidence for intraflagellar transport was provided around 25 years ago by experimental observations in Chlamydomonas of particles moving processively along the flagellum at constant speed.
source: The original evidence for this intraflagellar transport (IFT) was provided around 25 years ago by experimental observations in Chlamydomonas of particles moving processively along the flagellum at constant speed (Kozminski et al., 1993).
evidence: Stated with citation to the original experimental observation.

claim: IFT was hypothesized to play a role in flagellar length control by transporting building blocks to the tip of the flagellum.
source: Already at the time of its discovery, IFT was hypothesized to play a role in flagellar length control by transporting building blocks to the tip of the flagellum (Kozminski et al., 1993).
evidence: Stated with citation to the hypothesis at the time of IFT discovery.

claim: Kinesin-2 transports IFT particles from the flagellar base to tip (the anterograde direction).
source: IFT particles containing tubulin are transported along the flagellum by two different motor proteins: kinesin-2 transports IFT particles from the flagellar base to tip (the anterograde direction) whereas dynein carries IFT particles from the tip to the base (the retrograde direction).
evidence: Stated as a description of the motor protein function.

claim: Dynein carries IFT particles from the tip to the base (the retrograde direction).
source: IFT particles containing tubulin are transported along the flagellum by two different motor proteins: kinesin-2 transports IFT particles from the flagellar base to tip (the anterograde direction) whereas dynein carries IFT particles from the tip to the base (the retrograde direction).
evidence: Stated as a description of the motor protein function.

claim: Flagellar proteins are continually exchanged with those localized to the basal body of the flagellum.
source: As shown in subsequent work (Song and Dentler, 2001; Marshall and Rosenbaum, 2001; Buisson et al., 2013), these flagellar proteins are continually exchanged with those localized to the basal body of the flagellum, represented schematically in Figure 2a as a basal pool.
evidence: Stated with citations and reference to schematic figure.

claim: In the balance point model, there is a continual competition between assembly and disassembly.
source: In the balance point model, there is a continual competition between assembly and disassembly, and either the rate of assembly, the rate of disassembly, or both, may be length-dependent.
evidence: Stated as a description of the balance point model.

claim: The steady-state length in the balance point model is determined by the point at which the assembly and disassembly processes come into balance.
source: The steady-state length is determined by the point at which the assembly and disassembly processes come into balance.
evidence: Stated as a description of how steady-state is achieved in the balance point model.

claim: The balance point model has been considered primarily for a single flagellum with assembly being the length dependent process.
source: Up to now, the balance point model has been considered primarily for a single flagellum and the focus has been on assembly being the length dependent process that leads to length control (Marshall and Rosenbaum, 2001).
evidence: Stated with citation describing the historical focus of the model.

claim: None of the candidate models assuming constant disassembly capture the rapid length equalization observed experimentally.
source: With respect to the short time behavior, we find that none of the candidate models assuming constant disassembly capture the rapid length equalization observed experimentally.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the theoretical analysis.

claim: If an external control mechanism is added that replenishes proteins lost due to severing over a slower timescale, the constant disassembly models within our model space fail to control lengths at all.
source: Moreover, if an external control mechanism is added that replenishes proteins lost due to severing over a slower timescale, the constant disassembly models within our model space fail to control lengths at all.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the theoretical analysis.

claim: Microtubule-depolymerizing proteins have been observed within the flagellum.
source: Motivated by experimental observations of microtubule-depolymerizing proteins within the flagellum (Piao et al., 2009; Luo et al., 2011; Hilton et al., 2013), we subsequently consider a model in which the disassembly rate is dependent on the local concentration of a depolymerizing protein at the flagellar tips.
evidence: Stated with citations to experimental observations.

claim: The model with length-dependent disassembly is consistent with the rapid length equalization observed in experiments.
source: We find that this model is consistent with the rapid length equalization observed in experiments.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the model analysis.

claim: Upon adding a control mechanism on protein levels in the basal protein pool, the model is able to capture the slow return to the original steady-state lengths observed experimentally.
source: Further, upon adding a control mechanism on protein levels in the basal protein pool, the model is able to capture the slow return to the original steady-state lengths observed experimentally.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the model analysis.

claim: The injection rate of IFT particles in Chlamydomonas is length-dependent.
source: It is known from experiments that the injection rate of IFT particles in Chlamydomonas is length-dependent (Dentler, 2005).
evidence: Stated with citation to experimental observation.

claim: Length-dependent injection is a consequence of mass action kinetics of proteins available in limiting amounts.
source: In this section, we show how length-dependent injection is a consequence of mass action kinetics of proteins available in limiting amounts.
evidence: Stated as a result to be demonstrated in the section.

claim: Kinesin-2 has been shown to undergo ballistic transport in the anterograde direction and diffusive motion in the retrograde direction.
source: Kinesin-2 has been shown to undergo ballistic transport in the anterograde direction and diffusive motion in the retrograde direction (Chien et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated with citation to experimental observation.

claim: The timescale of flagellar length dynamics is of the order of 10 min.
source: The timescale of flagellar length dynamics, for example the recovery time after severing, is of the order of 10 min, whereas the molecular motors involved in IFT take at most tens of seconds to traverse the length of the flagellum by either ballistic or diffusive motion.
evidence: Stated as an observation about the timescales involved.

claim: Molecular motors involved in IFT take at most tens of seconds to traverse the length of the flagellum by either ballistic or diffusive motion.
source: The timescale of flagellar length dynamics, for example the recovery time after severing, is of the order of 10 min, whereas the molecular motors involved in IFT take at most tens of seconds to traverse the length of the flagellum by either ballistic or diffusive motion.
evidence: Stated as an observation about the timescales involved.

claim: The severing experiments contain two separate timescales: an initial fast timescale of 10–20 min over which the flagellar lengths first equalize, followed by a slower timescale of 60–90 min over which the lengths increase simultaneously to their original lengths.
source: As shown in Figure 1b, the severing experiments contain two separate timescales. There is an initial fast timescale of 10–20 min over which the flagellar lengths first equalize, followed by a slower timescale of 60–90 min over which the lengths increase simultaneously to their original lengths.
evidence: Stated with reference to experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The quasi-steady state assumption of flux balance together with mass action kinetics of injection imply that J = (k_on M)/(1 + k_on L/v + k_on L^2/2D).
source: As shown in Materials and methods, the quasi-steady state assumption of flux balance together with mass action kinetics of injection expressed in Equation 1 imply that
evidence: Stated as a derived result with reference to Materials and methods.

claim: The quasi-steady state assumption used to derive Equation 4 is validated by comparing to stochastic simulations.
source: We have validated the quasi-steady state assumption used to derive Equation 4 by comparing the IFT particle flux and the concentration of diffusing motors in the flagellum to the results of stochastic simulations (see Appendix 1), in which the dynamics of motors as well as the dynamics of microtubule assembly are taken into account explicitly; see Figure 2b.
evidence: Stated with reference to simulations and figure showing comparison.

claim: The limiting-pool mechanism alone is insufficient for the simultaneous length control of two flagella.
source: Whereas for a single flagellum the limiting-pool mechanism leads to a stable steady-state length, we show next that this mechanism is insufficient for the simultaneous length control of two flagella.
evidence: Stated as a finding to be demonstrated.

claim: Severing experiments illustrate that the flagella are coupled.
source: Severing experiments illustrate that the flagella are coupled.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of experimental observations.

claim: In the case of separate pools of both motors and tubulin, the unsevered flagellum does not decrease in length.
source: In the case of separate pools of both motors and tubulin (Equations 44 and 45), the unsevered flagellum does not decrease in length.
evidence: Stated with reference to equations and shown in Figure 3b(i).

claim: When only motors are shared, the flagellar lengths do not equalize after severing.
source: When only motors are shared (Equations 49 and 50), the flagellar lengths do not equalize after severing.
evidence: Stated with reference to equations and shown in Figure 3b(ii).

claim: When only tubulin is shared, the flagellar lengths do not equalize after severing.
source: When only tubulin is shared (Equations 56 and 57), the flagellar lengths do not equalize after severing.
evidence: Stated with reference to equations and shown in Figure 3b(iii).

claim: When both tubulin and motors are shared, there is no unique steady-state.
source: When both tubulin and motors are shared (Equations 58 and 59), there is no unique steady-state. The difference between the two flagellar lengths undergoes a random walk, as shown by the mean square displacement (inset, average over 10 runs).
evidence: Stated with reference to equations and shown in Figure 3b(iv).

claim: The constant disassembly models do not yield the rapid length equalization observed experimentally.
source: As we shall see, the constant disassembly models within our model space do not yield the rapid length equalization observed experimentally.
evidence: Stated as a summary of findings to be demonstrated.

claim: If the lengths are in steady-state prior to severing, they are also in steady-state immediately after severing in constant disassembly models.
source: As shown in Figure 3b and considered next on a case-by-case basis, if the lengths are in steady-state prior to severing, they are also in steady-state immediately after severing as well so that no length equalization occurs.
evidence: Stated as a finding with reference to figure showing simulations.

claim: In constant disassembly models, the assembly and disassembly rates depend only on free protein levels in the basal protein pools, which are unaffected by severing.
source: This is because in these models the assembly and disassembly rates depend only on free protein levels in the basal protein pools, which are unaffected by severing.
evidence: Stated as an explanation for why constant disassembly models fail to capture length equalization.

claim: The case of separate tubulin pools and individual motor pools is fundamentally inconsistent with the coupling observed in severing experiments.
source: The case of separate tubulin pools and individual motor pools leads to two uncoupled instances of (6). This is fundamentally inconsistent with the coupling observed in severing experiments, in particular the significant decrease in the length of the unsevered flagellum (Figure 3b(i)).
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from model analysis with reference to figure.

claim: The shared tubulin, separate motors model does not capture the length equalization observed in severing experiments.
source: As shown in Figure 3b(iii) and Figure 3—video 2, this model does not capture the length equalization observed in severing experiments and therefore may be ruled out.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion with reference to figure and video.

claim: Sharing all biomolecules between filaments does not yield simultaneous length control, a conclusion also reached in the context of actin filaments.
source: Indeed, a similar conclusion was reached in the context of actin filaments (Mohapatra et al., 2017), in which it was observed that sharing all biomolecules between filaments does not yield simultaneous length control.
evidence: Stated with citation to previous work on actin filaments.

claim: Regardless of the manner in which tubulin and motors are shared between flagella, the constant disassembly models are unable to explain the results of severing experiments.
source: The above analysis shows that, regardless of the manner in which tubulin and motors are shared between flagella, the constant disassembly models we have considered are unable to explain the results of severing experiments.
evidence: Stated as a summary conclusion from the analysis.

claim: Using cycloheximide at the time of severing to block the synthesis of new proteins results in shorter flagella that do not recover to their original lengths.
source: This was shown experimentally by using cycloheximide at the time of severing to block the synthesis of new proteins (Rosenbaum et al., 1969), resulting in shorter flagella that did not recover to their original lengths.
evidence: Stated with citation to experimental observation.

claim: Adding an external control mechanism that replenishes protein levels does not lead to length equalization in constant disassembly models.
source: However, as we next show, adding such a control mechanism on free proteins levels in the basal pool does not lead to length equalization. Instead, in this case the constant disassembly models we have considered completely fail to control lengths.
evidence: Stated as a finding to be demonstrated.

claim: External control mechanisms that drive free protein levels to target values destabilize flagellar lengths in constant disassembly models.
source: Therefore, this external control mechanism actually destabilizes the flagellar lengths (see Figure 3—videos 4—6 to observe this destabilization for various modes of coupling).
evidence: Stated as a conclusion with reference to videos showing destabilization.

claim: The argument that external control destabilizes lengths is general and does not depend on the details of the control mechanism.
source: Note that although we have used the simplest case of linear feedback Equations 18 and 19 to illustrate the point, this argument is general and does not depend on the details of the control mechanism.
evidence: Stated as a clarification of the generality of the result.

claim: Experiments on mutants in which IFT was disabled showed constant disassembly rates.
source: The assumption of a constant disassembly rate was based on experiments on mutants in which IFT was disabled (Marshall et al., 2005).
evidence: Stated with citation to experimental observation.

claim: Subsequent experiments in organisms with intact IFT led to 50-fold greater disassembly rates than those measured in the absence of IFT.
source: However, subsequent experiments in organisms with intact IFT led to 50-fold greater disassembly rates than those measured in the absence of IFT (Ludington et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated with citation to experimental observation.

claim: Some kinesin species (e.g. kinesin-13) participate in microtubule disassembly.
source: Experimental observations that some kinesin species (e.g. kinesin-13) participate in microtubule disassembly (Piao et al., 2009) provide a potential biochemical basis for IFT-dependent disassembly.
evidence: Stated with citation to experimental observation.

claim: The concentration-dependent disassembly model yields simultaneous length control and length equalization after severing.
source: This model yields simultaneous length control and length equalization after severing (Figure 4 and Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: Stated as a finding with reference to figure and video.

claim: Concentration-dependent disassembly yields simultaneous length control when all biomolecules are shared between flagella.
source: Therefore, concentration-dependent disassembly yields simultaneous length control when all biomolecules are shared between flagella and is consistent with the rapid length equalization observed after severing Figure 4b.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion with reference to figure.

claim: The presence of a concentration gradient is a critical ingredient in the concentration-dependent disassembly model.
source: The presence of a concentration gradient is a critical ingredient in this model and here it is achieved by ballistic transport to the flagellar tip with diffusive return.
evidence: Stated as an explanation of the model mechanism.

claim: The concentration gradient makes the disassembly rates length-dependent and yields independent equations for the steady-state lengths.
source: The concentration gradient makes the disassembly rates length-dependent and yields independent equations for the steady-state lengths.
evidence: Stated as an explanation of how the model achieves length control.

claim: The concentration-dependent disassembly model allows for an external control mechanism on protein levels in the basal pool, unlike the constant disassembly models.
source: Another feature of the concentration-dependent disassembly model is that it allows for an external control mechanism on protein levels in the basal pool, unlike the constant disassembly models we have considered.
evidence: Stated as a distinguishing feature of the model.

claim: Stability of the N-flagella solution follows from analyzing the linearized equations.
source: Stability follows from analyzing the linearized equations, as shown in Appendix 3.
evidence: Stated with reference to appendix for the derivation.

claim: Sharing both tubulin and motors leads to an indeterminate system of equations in constant disassembly models regardless of the details of the model.
source: In our initial exploration, in which we take the disassembly rate to be constant, we find that sharing both tubulin and motors leads to an indeterminate system of equations regardless of the details of the model, whereas sharing either tubulin or motors, but not both, results in simultaneous length control of both flagella.
evidence: Stated as a summary of findings in the Discussion.

claim: By examining the steady-state lengths immediately before and after severing and accounting for depletion in both the tubulin and motor pools, none of the constant disassembly models are able to capture the length equalization observed in experiments.
source: However, by examining the steady-state lengths immediately before and after severing and accounting for depletion in both the tubulin and motor pools, we observe that none of the constant disassembly models we have considered are able to capture the length equalization observed in experiments.
evidence: Stated as a summary of findings in the Discussion.

claim: The active disassembly model agrees with the results of severing experiments.
source: This model agrees with the results of severing experiments.
evidence: Stated as a summary of findings in the Discussion.

claim: The linear concentration gradient generated by diffusion acts as a ruler, but must be combined with a mechanism such as concentration-dependent disassembly.
source: As suggested by the title of Hendel et al. (2018), the linear concentration gradient generated by diffusion acts as a ruler. However, in our model diffusion must be combined with a mechanism such as concentration-dependent disassembly; the constant disassembly models we have considered are inconsistent with severing experiments regardless of whether the motor dynamics are ballistic, diffusive, or some combination.
evidence: Stated as a clarification of the model mechanism with reference to previous work.

claim: The model of Hendel et al. (2018) achieves length equalization by replenishing the total number of motors on the flagellum through an additional control mechanism that instantaneously adds the motors lost through severing back into the basal pool.
source: Whereas these equations do not lead to length equalization after severing in the case of no protein replenishment (Figure 3b(iii)), the model of Hendel et al. (2018) achieves length equalization by replenishing the total number of motors on the flagellum, that is through an additional control mechanism that instantaneously adds the motors lost through severing back into the basal pool.
evidence: Stated as a description of the difference between models with citation.

claim: The importance of replenishment for the Hendel et al. model appears to be inconsistent with severing experiments that show length equalization occurs even when protein synthesis is blocked using cyclohexamide.
source: The importance of replenishment for the model appears to be inconsistent with severing experiments that show length equalization occurs even when protein synthesis is blocked using cyclohexamide (Rosenbaum et al., 1969).
evidence: Stated as a critique with citation to experimental observation.

claim: The concentration-dependent disassembly model achieves length equalization with or without replenishment.
source: In contrast, the concentration-dependent disassembly model achieves length equalization with or without replenishment (Figure 4b and Figure 4c).
evidence: Stated as a distinguishing feature with reference to figures.

claim: The model predicts that the tubulin and depolymerizer pools must both be shared for the concentration-dependent disassembly model to capture the rapid length equalization observed.
source: Our model predicts that the tubulin and depolymerizer pools must both be shared for the concentration-dependent disassembly model to capture the rapid length equalization observed (Appendix 3).
evidence: Stated as a prediction from the model with reference to appendix.

claim: Having a protein that is not exchanged can provide simultaneous length control by a limiting-pool mechanism, but it introduces asymmetries that contradict the length equalization observed in severing experiments.
source: In particular, having a protein that is not exchanged can provide simultaneous length control by a limiting-pool mechanism, but it introduces asymmetries that contradict the length equalization observed in severing experiments.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the model analysis.

claim: According to the model, the depolymerizer active in length control is not uniformly distributed along the flagellum; its concentration increases toward the flagellar tip.
source: For example, according to our model the depolymerizer active in length control is not uniformly distributed along the flagellum; its concentration increases toward the flagellar tip.
evidence: Stated as a prediction from the model.

claim: The depolymerizer concentration profile could be tested experimentally by fluorescently labeling candidate depolymerizers and studying their concentration profiles along the flagellum.
source: This could be tested experimentally by fluorescently labeling candidate depolymerizers and studying their concentration profiles along the flagellum as recently done to characterize the concentration profile of kinesin-13 in Giardia (McInally et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated as a suggested experimental test with citation to similar work.

claim: The essential ingredient that leads to simultaneous length control is the presence of a depolymerizing protein with a concentration gradient along the flagellum.
source: In our model the essential ingredient that leads to simultaneous length control is the presence of a depolymerizing protein with a concentration gradient along the flagellum.
evidence: Stated as a summary of the key model feature.

claim: The main results are independent of the detailed form of the concentration gradient and how it is generated.
source: Although here as proof of principle this concentration gradient is achieved by the mechanism of ballistic-to-diffusive motion, our main results are independent of the detailed form of this concentration gradient and how it is generated.
evidence: Stated as a clarification of the generality of the results.

claim: The model allows for depolymerizers with nonlinear concentration profiles and different patterns of motion.
source: As shown in Appendix 3—figure 3b, our model allows for depolymerizers with nonlinear concentration profiles and different patterns of motion, for example exponential concentration distributions such as those recently observed in Giardia (McInally et al., 2019) and those generated by motile proteins that bind and unbind to cytoskeletal filaments, as theorized in the context of actin-myosin systems (Naoz et al., 2008; Orly et al., 2014; Pinkoviezky and Gov, 2014; Pinkoviezky and Gov, 2017; Yochelis et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated with reference to appendix figure and citations to experimental and theoretical work.

claim: The main results do not rely on many of the details of the model.
source: Our main results do not rely on many of the details of the model.
evidence: Stated as a summary of the robustness of the findings.

claim: Although the model takes depolymerase activity to depend linearly on concentration, the model generalizes to the non-linear case in a straightforward manner.
source: Although here we have taken depolymerase activity to depend linearly on concentration, the model generalizes to the non-linear case in a straightforward manner.
evidence: Stated as a clarification of the model's generality.

claim: In Chlamydomonas severing experiments have shown that depletion effects are important.
source: Finally, although in principle concentration-dependent disassembly yields length control even the case that all biomolecules are in excess, in Chlamydomonas severing experiments have shown that depletion effects are important (e.g. cyclohexamide treatment yields short flagella that do not return to their original steady-state lengths [Rosenbaum et al., 1969]).
evidence: Stated with citation to experimental observation.

claim: Within the model, depletion effects arise through limiting-pools of proteins.
source: Within our model such depletion effects arise through limiting-pools of proteins, and in Appendix 3 we explain that limiting pools of IFT motors are necessary for agreement with data whereas tubulin may either be limited or in excess.
evidence: Stated as an explanation of how the model captures depletion effects.

claim: Limiting pools of IFT motors are necessary for agreement with data whereas tubulin may either be limited or in excess.
source: Within our model such depletion effects arise through limiting-pools of proteins, and in Appendix 3 we explain that limiting pools of IFT motors are necessary for agreement with data whereas tubulin may either be limited or in excess.
evidence: Stated as a finding with reference to appendix.

claim: Such a depolymerizer (ballistically transported to the tip and then diffusing back) has yet to be identified in Chlamydomonas.
source: Although our results suggest that having a depolymerizer—one which is ballistically transported to the tip and then diffuses back—provides an appealing model for simultaneous length control, such a depolymeriser has yet to be identified in Chlamydomonas.
evidence: Stated as an acknowledgment of the current state of experimental knowledge.

claim: Recent experiments have shown kinesin-13 to be involved in length control in Giardia.
source: While recent experiments have shown kinesin-13 to be involved in length control in Giardia (McInally et al., 2019), the observation that only negligible amounts of flagellar kinesin-13 are present at steady-state (Wang et al., 2013) appears to preclude it from being the candidate depolymerizer of our model.
evidence: Stated with citation to experimental observation.

claim: Only negligible amounts of flagellar kinesin-13 are present at steady-state in Chlamydomonas.
source: While recent experiments have shown kinesin-13 to be involved in length control in Giardia (McInally et al., 2019), the observation that only negligible amounts of flagellar kinesin-13 are present at steady-state (Wang et al., 2013) appears to preclude it from being the candidate depolymerizer of our model.
evidence: Stated with citation to experimental observation.

claim: Aurora-like kinase CALK has been shown to influence disassembly through its state of phosphorylation.
source: Other candidates include aurora-like kinase CALK, which has been shown to influence disassembly through its state of phosphorylation (Luo et al., 2011; Cao et al., 2013), and CNK2, a NIMA-related protein kinase known to localize to flagella (Bradley and Quarmby, 2005) whose absence yields Chlamydomonas with abnormally long flagella and decreased disassembly rates (Hilton et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated with citations to experimental observations.

claim: CNK2 is a NIMA-related protein kinase known to localize to flagella.
source: Other candidates include aurora-like kinase CALK, which has been shown to influence disassembly through its state of phosphorylation (Luo et al., 2011; Cao et al., 2013), and CNK2, a NIMA-related protein kinase known to localize to flagella (Bradley and Quarmby, 2005) whose absence yields Chlamydomonas with abnormally long flagella and decreased disassembly rates (Hilton et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated with citation to experimental observation.

claim: Absence of CNK2 yields Chlamydomonas with abnormally long flagella and decreased disassembly rates.
source: Other candidates include aurora-like kinase CALK, which has been shown to influence disassembly through its state of phosphorylation (Luo et al., 2011; Cao et al., 2013), and CNK2, a NIMA-related protein kinase known to localize to flagella (Bradley and Quarmby, 2005) whose absence yields Chlamydomonas with abnormally long flagella and decreased disassembly rates (Hilton et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated with citation to experimental observation.

claim: A promising avenue to further test the active disassembly model is to study length fluctuations about steady-state.
source: On the side of theory, a promising avenue to further test the active disassembly model and discriminate between different possibilities is to study length fluctuations about steady-state.
evidence: Stated as a suggestion for future theoretical work.

claim: The fluctuation spectra of each model provides a signature that can be used to assess both the general model framework and to test the autocorrelation timescales predicted by each model.
source: The fluctuation spectra of each model provides a signature that can be used to assess both the general model framework and to test the autocorrelation timescales predicted by each model (Amir and Balaban, 2018).
evidence: Stated with citation as a suggested approach for model testing.

claim: The flagellar geometry is fully described by its length given a constant cross-sectional area.
source: Given the highly regular structure of the axoneme revealed by cryo-electron microscopy (Bui et al., 2008; Barber et al., 2012), we assume a constant cross-sectional area in which case the flagellar geometry is fully described by its length.
evidence: Stated as a modeling assumption with citations to structural studies.

claim: The timescale of 15 min is long compared to the few tens of seconds needed for molecular motors to traverse the flagellum in IFT, which justifies the quasi-steady state approximation.
source: This timescale is long compared to the few tens of seconds needed for molecular motors to traverse the flagellum in IFT, which justifies a posteriori our approximation of IFT as a quasi-steady state process.
evidence: Stated as a justification for the modeling assumption.

claim: The formulation of Hendel et al. (2018) is very similar to Equations 56 and 57 derived in the case of shared tubulin pools and separate motor pools with constant disassembly.
source: As we describe in Materials and methods, the formulation of Hendel et al. (2018) is very similar to Equations 56 and 57 derived in the case of shared tubulin pools and separate motor pools with constant disassembly.
evidence: Stated as a comparison between models.
